name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q01 - Sequence of acid catalysed dehydration of ethanol

questiontext.text:
Consider the following elementary stages involved in the mechanism of the acid-catalysed dehydration of ethanol to form ethene at \(443\text{ K}\):

I. Deprotonation of carbocation to form ethene
II. Elimination of a water molecule to form ethyl carbocation (rate-determining step)
III. Protonation of ethanol to form ethyl oxonium ion

Which of the following represents the correct chronological sequence of these mechanistic stages?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle of Acid-Catalysed Dehydration
Acid-catalysed dehydration of primary alcohols such as ethanol proceeds via an \(E1\)-type elimination pathway involving protonation, carbocation formation, and subsequent elimination of a proton.

Step 2: Identification of Initial Protonation
In the first stage, the unshared electron pair on the oxygen atom of ethanol attacks a proton supplied by the acid catalyst (\(\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\)). This fast reversible step yields the protonated alcohol species, the ethyl oxonium ion (\(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}_2^+\)).

Step 3: Identification of Rate-Determining Carbocation Generation
In the second stage, the carbon–oxygen bond undergoes heterolytic cleavage with the loss of a neutral water molecule. This slow, rate-determining step generates the ethyl carbocation (\(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2^+\)).

Step 4: Deprotonation to Yield Alkene
In the final stage, a base (such as water) removes a \(\beta\)-proton from the carbocation intermediate, yielding the carbon–carbon double bond of ethene (\(\text{CH}_2=\text{CH}_2\)) and regenerating the proton catalyst.

Final Answer:
The correct chronological sequence of the mechanistic stages is protonation of ethanol to form the ethyl oxonium ion, followed by elimination of a water molecule to generate the ethyl carbocation, followed by deprotonation to yield ethene (III → II → I).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q02 - Sequential events in industrial fermentation of ethanol

questiontext.text:
The following biological and chemical events take place during the production of ethanol from ripe grapes by fermentation:

I. Yeast enzyme zymase ferments glucose and fructose into ethanol and carbon dioxide.
II. Ripe grapes are crushed, bringing the sugary juice into contact with yeast residing on the outer skin.
III. The action of zymase is naturally arrested as alcohol content exceeds \(14\%\).
IV. Yeast enzyme invertase hydrolyses sucrose into glucose and fructose.

What is the correct chronological sequence of these stages during fermentation?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Initiation of Fermentation by Physical Contact
As grapes ripen, their sugar content increases while wild yeast grows on the skins. The process starts when grapes are crushed, allowing the sugars and the enzymes from yeast to come into direct physical contact.

Step 2: Enzymatic Inversion of Sucrose
Once in contact, the enzyme invertase secreted by yeast catalyses the hydrolysis of sucrose (\(\text{C}_{12}\text{H}_{22}\text{O}_{11}\)) into glucose and fructose (\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6\)).

Step 3: Anaerobic Glycolytic Cleavage by Zymase
Under strictly anaerobic conditions, the enzyme complex zymase ferments the resulting glucose and fructose into ethanol (\(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}\)) and gaseous carbon dioxide (\(\text{CO}_2\)).

Step 4: Biological Inhibition at Elevated Alcohol Concentration
Ethanol is toxic to yeast at elevated levels; hence, the enzymatic activity of zymase becomes inhibited once the ethanol concentration reaches approximately \(14\%\), terminating the natural fermentation process.

Final Answer:
The correct chronological order of the process is crushing of ripe grapes, followed by hydrolysis of sucrose by invertase, followed by fermentation of hexoses by zymase, and finally inhibition of zymase above \(14\%\) ethanol (II → IV → I → III).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q03 - Sequential stages in phenol manufacture from cumene

questiontext.text:
The industrial manufacture of phenol from cumene involves several sequential stages:

I. Aerobic oxidation of cumene (isopropylbenzene) in the presence of air.
II. Acid-catalysed cleavage of cumene hydroperoxide using dilute mineral acid.
III. Accumulation of cumene hydroperoxide intermediate.
IV. Separation and isolation of phenol along with the valuable by-product propanone.

Which of the following represents the correct logical sequence of these stages in the industrial process?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Industrial Importance and Starting Reagents
Most worldwide production of phenol utilizes cumene (isopropylbenzene) as the starting hydrocarbon material due to high atom economy and commercial co-production of propanone.

Step 2: Free Radical Oxidation
The process begins with the aerial oxidation of cumene, where molecular oxygen selectively attacks the tertiary benzylic carbon atom.

Step 3: Hydroperoxide Intermediate Formation
This free-radical auto-oxidation produces cumene hydroperoxide (\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{OOH}\)) as a stable isolable intermediate.

Step 4: Acid Cleavage and Product Isolation
Cumene hydroperoxide is subsequently treated with dilute aqueous acid, initiating rearrangement and cleavage into phenol and propanone (acetone). Fractional distillation completes the process by isolating both pure products.

Final Answer:
The correct logical sequence is oxidation of cumene in air, formation of cumene hydroperoxide, cleavage with dilute acid, and separation of phenol and propanone (I → III → II → IV).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q04 - Synthetic steps from benzene to phenol via sulphonation

questiontext.text:
Phenol can be synthesised in the laboratory from benzene through a series of chemical transformations:

I. Fusion of benzenesulphonic acid with molten sodium hydroxide.
II. Acidification of the phenoxide salt with aqueous mineral acid to liberate phenol.
III. Electrophilic aromatic substitution of benzene with oleum to yield benzenesulphonic acid.
IV. Conversion of the sulphonate intermediate into sodium phenoxide.

Select the correct sequential order of operations required to carry out this complete conversion.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Introduction of the Leaving Group on Benzene
Benzene is initially subjected to electrophilic aromatic sulphonation by treating it with oleum (fuming sulphuric acid), producing benzenesulphonic acid (\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{SO}_3\text{H}\)).

Step 2: Alkali Fusion
The benzenesulphonic acid is then heated and fused with molten sodium hydroxide at high temperature.

Step 3: Formation of Phenoxide Intermediate
During alkali fusion, nucleophilic displacement of the sulphonate group occurs, generating sodium phenoxide (\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{ONa}\)) along with sodium sulphite.

Step 4: Acidification to Liberate Free Phenol
Finally, the basic reaction mixture containing sodium phenoxide is acidified with dilute mineral acid (such as \(\text{HCl}\) or \(\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\)), protonating the phenoxide ion to yield free phenol.

Final Answer:
The correct sequential order of operations is sulphonation of benzene with oleum, fusion with molten sodium hydroxide, formation of sodium phenoxide, and final acidification to yield phenol (III → I → IV → II).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q05 - Mechanistic stages in intermolecular dehydration to ether

questiontext.text:
When ethanol is heated with concentrated sulphuric acid at \(413\text{ K}\), bimolecular dehydration gives ethoxyethane via an \(\text{S}_\text{N}2\) mechanism involving the following stages:

I. Deprotonation of the dialkyloxonium ion to regenerate \(\text{H}^+\) and release ethoxyethane.
II. Protonation of an ethanol molecule by the protic acid to form an ethyl oxonium ion.
III. Nucleophilic attack by the oxygen of a second unprotonated ethanol molecule on the \(\alpha\)-carbon of the protonated alcohol with concerted departure of water.

What is the correct chronological sequence of these mechanistic steps?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Role of Temperature and Mechanism Overview
At \(413\text{ K}\), substitution predominates over elimination because of the lower temperature. Primary alcohols like ethanol undergo bimolecular nucleophilic substitution (\(\text{S}_\text{N}2\)) to form symmetrical ethers.

Step 2: Protonation Stage
The reaction begins when an ethanol molecule acts as a Brønsted base and accepts a proton from \(\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\), transforming the poor hydroxyl leaving group (\(-\text{OH}\)) into an excellent neutral leaving group (\(-\text{OH}_2^+\)) in the ethyl oxonium ion (\(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}_2^+\)).

Step 3: Bimolecular Nucleophilic Attack
In the second stage, a second, neutral ethanol molecule acts as a nucleophile, using a lone pair on its oxygen atom to attack the back side of the \(\alpha\)-carbon in the protonated alcohol. The water molecule is displaced concertedly via an \(\text{S}_\text{N}2\) pathway, producing a protonated ether intermediate, the diethyloxonium ion (\(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\overset{+}{\text{O}}\text{HCH}_2\text{CH}_3\)).

Step 4: Deprotonation Stage
Finally, the oxonium intermediate loses a proton to a solvent molecule or conjugate base, regenerating the acidic catalyst and providing the final product, diethyl ether (ethoxyethane).

Final Answer:
The correct chronological sequence is protonation of ethanol, followed by nucleophilic displacement of water by a second ethanol molecule, followed by loss of a proton to yield ethoxyethane (II → III → I).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q06 - Progression of intermediates in hydroboration oxidation of propene

questiontext.text:
During the conversion of propene into propan-1-ol via hydroboration–oxidation, several organoboron species are sequentially formed:

I. Dipropylborane, \((\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2)_2\text{BH}\)
II. Propan-1-ol and boric acid, \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH} + \text{B(OH)}_3\)
III. Monopropylborane, \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{BH}_2\)
IV. Tripropylborane, \((\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2)_3\text{B}\)

What is the correct sequential order of appearance of these species during the overall reaction?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Regiochemical Principles of Hydroboration
Diborane adds across the carbon–carbon double bond of propene such that the boron atom attaches regioselectively to the less substituted \(sp^2\) carbon atom carrying the larger number of hydrogen atoms.

Step 2: Initial Monoadduct Formation
The first equivalent of propene reacts with a borane unit (\(\text{BH}_3\)) to form monopropylborane (\(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{BH}_2\)).

Step 3: Successive Additions to Boron
Because monopropylborane retains two active \(\text{B}-\text{H}\) bonds, it reacts with a second molecule of propene to yield dipropylborane (\((\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2)_2\text{BH}\)), which then reacts with a third molecule of propene to yield tripropylborane (\((\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2)_3\text{B}\)).

Step 4: Alkaline Peroxide Oxidation
In the second stage of the reaction, tripropylborane is oxidised by hydrogen peroxide in alkaline aqueous medium (\(\text{H}_2\text{O}_2/\text{OH}^-\)), cleaving all three carbon–boron bonds to deliver three moles of propan-1-ol and one mole of boric acid (\(\text{B(OH)}_3\)).

Final Answer:
The correct sequence of appearance of species is monopropylborane, followed by dipropylborane, followed by tripropylborane, and finally propan-1-ol with boric acid (III → I → IV → II).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q07 - Mechanistic steps in Reimer Tiemann formylation of phenol

questiontext.text:
Consider the following steps involved in the conversion of phenol into salicylaldehyde via the Reimer–Tiemann reaction:

I. Alkaline hydrolysis of the substituted benzal chloride intermediate.
II. Generation of electrophilic dichlorocarbene (\(:\!\text{CCl}_2\)) by the action of aqueous \(\text{NaOH}\) on chloroform.
III. Final acidification of the sodium salt of salicylaldehyde with dilute mineral acid.
IV. Electrophilic attack of dichlorocarbene on the ortho position of the resonance-stabilised phenoxide ring.

Which of the following represents the correct chronological sequence of these steps?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Generation of Reactive Carbene Electrophile
Aqueous sodium hydroxide deprotonates chloroform (\(\text{CHCl}_3\)) to form the trichloromethyl carbanion, which readily loses a chloride ion by \(\alpha\)-elimination to produce neutral, electron-deficient dichlorocarbene (\(:\!\text{CCl}_2\)).

Step 2: Electrophilic Aromatic Attack
Phenol is simultaneously converted by \(\text{NaOH}\) into strongly activated phenoxide ion. The electron-rich phenoxide ring undergoes electrophilic attack by dichlorocarbene predominantly at the ortho position, forming an intermediate substituted benzal chloride species bearing a \(-\text{CHCl}_2\) group.

Step 3: Hydrolysis of the Benzal Chloride Group
In the strongly alkaline medium, the geminal dichloromethyl group (\(-\text{CHCl}_2\)) undergoes nucleophilic substitution by hydroxide ions followed by dehydration, generating an ortho-formyl phenoxide salt.

Step 4: Acidification to Salicylaldehyde
Acidification with dilute acid protonates the phenoxide oxygen to deliver the neutral final product, salicylaldehyde (2-hydroxybenzaldehyde).

Final Answer:
The correct chronological order of mechanistic events is generation of dichlorocarbene, attack of carbene on the phenoxide ring, alkaline hydrolysis of the benzal chloride intermediate, and acidification to free salicylaldehyde (II → IV → I → III).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q08 - Mechanism sequence of tertiary ether cleavage with hydrogen iodide

questiontext.text:
When tert-butyl methyl ether, \((\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}-\text{O}-\text{CH}_3\), is treated with concentrated hydrogen iodide (\(\text{HI}\)), the reaction proceeds via an \(\text{S}_\text{N}1\) pathway involving the following stages:

I. Nucleophilic capture of the tert-butyl carbocation by iodide ion (\(\text{I}^-\)) to form tert-butyl iodide.
II. Protonation of the ether oxygen atom by \(\text{HI}\) to form an oxonium ion.
III. Slow heterolytic cleavage of the tertiary \(\text{C}-\text{O}\) bond with departure of neutral methanol to produce a stable tert-butyl carbocation.

What is the correct chronological sequence of these steps?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Mechanistic Governing Principle
In ethers containing a tertiary alkyl group, cleavage does not follow the steric-controlled \(\text{S}_\text{N}2\) pathway seen in primary alkyl ethers. Instead, it proceeds through a carbocation-controlled unimolecular substitution pathway (\(\text{S}_\text{N}1\)).

Step 2: Protonation of the Ether Oxygen
The first step involves proton transfer from strongly acidic hydrogen iodide to the lone pair of the ether oxygen, establishing a rapid equilibrium to produce the methyl tert-butyl oxonium ion.

Step 3: Carbocation Generation via Leaving Group Departure
In the second, rate-determining step, departure of the neutral leaving group (methanol, \(\text{CH}_3\text{OH}\)) occurs readily because it creates an extraordinarily stable tertiary carbocation, the tert-butyl cation (\((\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}^+\)).

Step 4: Nucleophilic Combination
In the rapid final stage, the iodide ion (\(\text{I}^-\)) attacks the planar carbocation center to form tert-butyl iodide (\((\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}-\text{I}\)).

Final Answer:
The correct chronological sequence is protonation of the ether, followed by slow departure of methanol to generate the tert-butyl carbocation, followed by capture by iodide ion to give tert-butyl iodide (II → III → I).
